Week 1 — Is Your Job AI-Proof? Why FDEs Are the Career AI Can't Replace 🧠
Why the one engineering role that sits face-to-face with the client is the hardest for AI to replace.
AI writes code today. It still can't sit with a client and figure out what they actually need.

Everyone is asking "will AI take my job?" In this session you'll see what AI can already do in software, what it still can't, and why the Forward Deployed Engineer role is built on exactly the part it can't. You'll leave with a clear view of where to put your effort over the next year.
What a Forward Deployed Engineer is, explained from zero
The 5 skills of an FDE: Consulting, Data Engineering, AI, Software Engineering, Deployment
How the work splits in practice: about 50% consulting, 30% engineering, 20% AI
Live demo: AI writes an API, a pipeline and a Dockerfile in minutes. What it still gets wrong without the right requirements
Which engineering tasks AI is taking over, and which ones it can't (client trust, business judgment, deciding what to build)
A self-check across the 5 skills to see where you stand today
explain what an FDE does, and name the 2-3 skills you should build first.
Week 2 — A Day in the Life of a Forward Deployed Engineer 🧠
An hour-by-hour walk through what an FDE actually does in a normal working day.
Client call at 10, pipeline at 1, deployment at 5. See what an FDE's day really looks like.

Job descriptions never tell you what the work feels like. This session walks through one full FDE day using a real Uber/Ola project, from the first client call to the evening deployment, so you can decide whether this is the career for you.
Tech stack you'll see on screen:
Python, SQL, Kafka, Docker, GitHub, Kubernetes
10:00 Client call: the questions asked and the notes taken
13:00 Build time: a data pipeline and an AI feature being built
17:00 Deployment: shipping a change to a live system
The 7-step FDE lifecycle: Discover, Translate, Design, Prototype, Deploy, Operate, Deliver
Which of the 5 FDE skills is active at each hour of the day
What typically goes wrong in a day (changed requirements, bad data, a failed deployment) and how an FDE handles each
describe an FDE's week to a friend and decide whether you want this job.
Week 3 — Why Consulting is the Most Important Skill for an FDE 💼
Live demo of turning a vague client ask ("build us something like Uber") into a written technical plan, using the questions an FDE asks on a real discovery call.
The FDE skill companies pay the most for has nothing to do with writing code.

A brilliant engineer who skips discovery builds the wrong thing, fast. Watch a role-played client call where a vague ask becomes a clear plan, and take home the exact questions and template to do the same.
Ten discovery questions to ask before writing any code (users, volumes, data sources, existing systems, success numbers, constraints)
Finding out what data actually exists, where it lives and how clean it is
Turning business answers into technical requirements: data sources to connect, pipelines needed, AI features, apps and APIs, expected load
Drawing a first architecture diagram from the requirements (Rider App, Driver App, backend, Kafka, database, AI services)
Estimating effort and spotting the risky parts early
A one-page requirements template you can reuse on any client
How to say "no" or "not yet" without losing the client's trust
run a discovery call and leave with a written plan the client agrees to.
Week 4 — Live Traffic Pipeline with Kafka 🛠️
Build a real streaming pipeline, from thousands of simulated driver GPS pings to clean, queryable data.
Driver GPS and live traffic, flowing through Kafka into a clean database. Built on screen, not on slides.
AI is only as good as the data behind it. You'll watch a live streaming pipeline get built from scratch, including what happens when data arrives late, duplicated or wrong.
Apache Kafka, Python, PostgreSQL, SQL, Docker
Topics, partitions, producers, consumers and consumer groups
Why Kafka sits between the apps and the database instead of writing straight to it
Choosing a message key (driver ID) so one driver's events stay in order
A Python producer simulating thousands of drivers sending GPS pings
A consumer that validates and cleans the stream: schema checks, duplicates, missing values, late events
Sending bad messages to a dead-letter topic instead of losing them
Catching fake locations: distance between two pings (haversine) divided by the time gap gives an impossible speed
Loading clean data into PostgreSQL with idempotent upserts and an index for fast lookups
Offsets and delivery guarantees: what happens when a consumer crashes mid-stream and how it resumes
Reading consumer lag to see whether the pipeline is keeping up
build and debug a streaming pipeline that stays correct when messages are duplicated, late or out of order.
Week 5 — Real-Time AI Agents: How a Multi-Agent System Handles a Live Ride Request 🛠️
Build a team of AI agents that reacts to a live ride request, uses real-time data from the Week 4 pipeline, and decides what to do within seconds.
A rider taps "Book". A team of AI agents has 3 seconds to respond. Watch them work in real time.

Most agent demos are chatbots answering one question. Real products use agents that react to live events, call tools on live data, recover when something fails, and ask a human before risky actions. You'll build exactly that with LangChain and LangGraph, on top of the traffic pipeline you built in Week 4.
Python, LangChain, LangGraph, LangSmith, Kafka, PostgreSQL, Pydantic
What an agent really is: the loop of think → call a tool → read the result → decide the next step
How an agent differs from a single LLM call, and from a fixed workflow
Tools: plain Python functions with a schema that the model can call (nearby available drivers from PostgreSQL, live traffic speed for a zone, ETA from distance and live speed)
Structured output with Pydantic, so the agent returns data your code can trust
State, nodes, edges and conditional routing
The ride-request graph: Intake → Data → ETA → Driver-matching → Confirmation
The supervisor pattern: one agent routes work between specialist agents
Running steps in parallel (check drivers and traffic at the same time)
Event-driven triggers: a ride-request event arriving on Kafka starts one run of the graph
Streaming intermediate progress to the Rider App
Holding a time budget per request (3 seconds)
Failure handling: tool timeouts, stale driver data, invalid model output, with retries and fallback paths
Human-in-the-loop: pausing the graph for approval before a risky action such as a refund or driver reassignment
Memory and checkpoints: saving state per ride so a run can pause and resume
Tracing every step (LangSmith) to see why an agent made a decision
Tracking cost (tokens) and latency per request
The FDE judgment call: plain function vs. single agent vs. agent team
design and build a multi-agent workflow that reacts to live events, handles failures and keeps a human in control.
Week 6 — Git & GitHub: Working on a Client Project Without Breaking It 🛠️
The Git workflow FDE teams use so client work stays safe, reviewable and reversible.
Two engineers, one client project, zero overwritten code.

Everything that comes next in this series (APIs, Docker, CI/CD) sits on Git. This hands-on session shows the exact workflow an FDE follows, including the mistakes: a merge conflict made on purpose, and a bad commit tracked down and undone.
Branches: one branch per feature instead of editing
Staging, commits and meaningful commit messages
Pull requests, code review and merging on GitHub
and why secrets and keys must never be committed
Creating a merge conflict on purpose and resolving it
Merge vs. rebase, explained on a small example
A simple branching strategy for a client project
Finding the exact commit that broke the service with
Keeping a clean history and a good README so the client can take the project over
work on a shared codebase without overwriting anyone's work, and recover from a bad commit.
Week 7 — Backend API: Serving the AI to Real Apps 🛠️
Wrap the Week 5 agent system in a real API that the Rider App and Driver App can call.
An agent in a notebook is not a product. Put it behind an API and put it in front of a user.

See two apps and one backend connected live: a rider requests a trip, the agent team picks the driver, the driver's app receives it. This is the step where a prototype starts becoming something a person can tap.
Python, FastAPI, Pydantic, Server-Sent Events / WebSockets, pytest, LangGraph
Request and response models with Pydantic, and clear error responses (400, 404, 500, timeouts)
Basic authentication for the Rider and Driver apps (API keys or JWT)
Making it behave in real time
Building the LangGraph graph once at startup instead of on every request
Async endpoints, so many riders can be served at once
Streaming live progress to the Rider App with server-sent events or WebSockets
Setting and measuring a response-time budget (a driver matched in under 3 seconds)
Writing API tests with pytest and FastAPI's test client
Mocking the LLM and tool calls so tests are fast and repeatable (these tests are reused in Week 10)
Wiring the Rider App and Driver App to the same backend, and handling CORS
expose an AI workflow as a tested, documented API that real apps can use.
Week 8 — Docker: Package It Once, Run It Anywhere 🛠️
Containerize the API, the agent service, the database and Kafka so the app runs identically on any machine.
"It works on my laptop" is not good enough. Package the app once and run it anywhere.
Every client's environment is different. You'll watch the app fail on a clean machine, then run perfectly inside a container, and finish with the whole stack starting from one command.
Docker, Docker Compose, Python, PostgreSQL, Kafka
Images vs. containers, in plain words
Pulling, running, listing and removing containers; reading logs with
, line by line, for the Week 7 API
Layer caching: why the order of lines changes build time
Smaller images with slim base images and multi-stage builds
, running as a non-root user, and a container health check
Docker Compose: API + Kafka + PostgreSQL started with one command
Networking (containers finding each other by name) and volumes (keeping database data)
files, and keeping secrets out of the image
containerize an application and run the full stack on any machine with one command.
Week 9 — The AI Chatbot Built on Real Data 🛠️
Build a support chatbot that answers from real ride data instead of making things up, and learn when a chatbot is the wrong answer.
A chatbot that knows where your driver actually is.
Most chatbot demos fall apart on real questions. You'll build one that retrieves facts from the product's data before answering, test it with tricky questions, and set the limits it must never cross.
Python, LangChain, embeddings, a vector store (FAISS / Chroma / pgvector), PostgreSQL, FastAPI
Chunking policy documents (refund rules, FAQs) and turning them into embeddings
Storing them in a vector store and retrieving the most relevant chunks
Writing the prompt so the answer comes only from the retrieved text, with the source shown
Why "Where is my driver?" needs a tool that queries live ride data, not a document search
Giving the chatbot both: retrieval for policy questions, tools for live status
What the bot must refuse, and when it should hand over to a human
Building a small test set of tricky questions and scoring the bot on it, so you know when a change makes it worse
When a chatbot is the right answer and when a button or a form is better
build a chatbot that answers from your data, refuses what it should, and can be tested before a client sees it.
Week 10 — CI/CD with GitHub Actions: Merge Code, Watch It Go Live 🛠️
Build the pipeline that tests, builds and deploys the backend automatically on every merge.
No more manual deployments. Merge to GitHub and the app tests, builds and ships itself.
Manual releases are slow and risky. You'll watch a failing test block a bad release, then a good change travel all the way to the live app without anyone touching a server.
GitHub Actions, Docker, a container registry (GitHub Container Registry), pytest, Kubernetes
Running on every pull request and every merge to
Caching dependencies to make runs faster
Test: running the Week 7 pytest suite automatically, so a failing test blocks the merge
Build: building the Docker image and pushing it to a registry with a version tag
Deploy: rolling the new image out, staging first and then production
Keeping credentials in GitHub Secrets instead of the code
Branch protection with required checks, so the pipeline is mandatory
Environments with a manual approval step before production
Rolling back when something slips through
set up a pipeline where every merge is tested, built and deployed automatically, with a safety net.
Week 11 — Kubernetes and Safe Releases: Surviving Friday Rush Hour 🛠️
Deploy the containers on Kubernetes, break things on purpose, and release a new agent version without riders noticing.
One server crashes, traffic triples, a bad release goes out. And the app keeps running.
This is the "demo vs. real product" session. You'll simulate a Friday rush hour, kill a running pod, and ship a new agent version to a small slice of riders first, all live.
Pods, Deployments and Services, and how they fit together
Writing a Deployment in YAML and applying it with
ConfigMaps and Secrets for settings and keys
Resource requests and limits, so one service can't starve the others
Self-healing: kill a pod and watch Kubernetes bring it back
Autoscaling with the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler as traffic spikes
Release strategies compared: rolling, blue-green and canary
A canary release for the agent system: 5% of riders on the new agent version, compared with the old one on success rate, latency and cost, then decide
When not to use Kubernetes: a small pilot is often better served by one VM with Docker Compose
deploy a containerized app on Kubernetes, scale it, recover it, and release changes without downtime.
Week 12 — Operate & Deliver: Monitoring, Handover and Your FDE Roadmap 🛠️ 🧠
Add the dashboards, alerts and nightly reports a live product needs, hand it over to the client, and plan your own FDE path.
Shipping isn't the finish line. At 2am, someone has to know it broke.

The last two steps of the FDE lifecycle are Operate and Deliver. You'll see a live "incident" solved using only dashboards, run the client handover, and finish with your personal roadmap across the 5 FDE skills.
Prometheus, Grafana, Apache Airflow, Python, Kubernetes

Structured logs with a ride ID, so one ride can be traced across services
Agent quality: match success rate, tool failure rate, response time (p95) and cost per request
Spotting quality drift as real usage changes
Finding the cause of a live incident using only logs and dashboards
A nightly Airflow job (extract, clean, load, report) that turns a day of rides into a business report for the client

monitor a live AI system, respond to an incident, and hand a project over so the client can run it without you.
